SECTION 174A CATCH-UP CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

1-year or 2-year? Compare the Section 174A R&E catch-up election.

If your business capitalized and amortized domestic research and experimental (R&E) costs from 2022-2024 under the old Section 174 rules, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act gives you a one-time catch-up deduction for whatever balance you had not yet amortized — claimed on your 2025 return, either entirely in 2025 or split evenly across 2025 and 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-28). This tool compares the actual cash tax savings and the present value of each path, based on the numbers you enter.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Your remaining unamortized balance

The portion of your 2022-2024 domestic R&E costs not yet amortized as of the start of your first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024 — 2025, for a calendar-year filer. This is not the retroactive-amendment path (its election window closed July 6, 2026); it is the choice you still make on your 2025 return.

2. Expected taxable income and rate, before this deduction

2025

2026

Income can be negative — enter a negative number if you expect a loss year. Rates can differ between the two years; that difference is exactly what this tool is built to weigh.

3. Time value of money (optional)

Defaults to 6% — a middle-of-the-range planning assumption between a risk-free rate and a small business's typical cost of borrowed cash (not an IRS-published figure). Adjust it to your own cost of capital; a 0% rate compares the two paths on nominal dollars only.

Fill in your balance, income, and rates, then click Calculate.

Comparison

1-year: all in 2025

2-year: split 2025 / 2026

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates the cash tax effect of one deduction only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, self-employment or payroll tax, AMT, or state tax (state conformity to Section 174A varies).
  • Does not verify small-business eligibility. The $31 million average-gross-receipts test (2022-2024) is confirmed by you, not checked here.
  • No net operating loss (NOL) carryforward modeling. When a deduction exceeds a year's taxable income, this tool flags the excess but does not estimate what a resulting NOL is worth in a later year, the Section 172(a) 80%-of-taxable-income limitation, or state NOL rules.
  • Does not model the retroactive-amendment election. That separate path (amending 2022-2024 returns directly) had its own election window, which closed July 6, 2026.

Common questions

What is the Section 174A catch-up deduction?

A one-time deduction created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) for an eligible small business that had capitalized and was amortizing domestic research and experimental (R&E) costs from 2022-2024 under the old Section 174 rules. It covers whatever portion of those costs was not yet amortized by the start of the business's first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024 -- 2025, for a calendar-year filer -- and is claimed on that 2025 return.

Who counts as an "eligible small business" for this catch-up?

A business whose average annual gross receipts for 2022, 2023, and 2024 (including a controlled group's) were $31 million or less -- the same Section 448(c) gross-receipts test used elsewhere in the tax code. This calculator does not check your gross receipts against that threshold; confirm your own eligibility before relying on either election.

What is the difference between the 1-year and 2-year election?

Both are elected on the 2025 return under Rev. Proc. 2025-28. The 1-year option deducts the entire remaining unamortized balance in 2025. The 2-year option spreads it ratably over two years -- half in 2025, half in 2026. Taking it all in 2025 front-loads the tax savings, which is better if 2025's rate or income is expected to be higher than 2026's. Spreading it out is better if 2025's rate or income is expected to be lower -- for example a loss or near-breakeven year -- or if the rate is expected to rise in 2026.

What happens if the deduction is bigger than my taxable income for that year?

The excess does not disappear, but it also does not produce an immediate cash tax saving that year -- it can create or increase a net operating loss (NOL) instead. This calculator flags that clearly and caps the current-year cash saving at that year's taxable income before the deduction. It does not model NOL carryforward value, the 80%-of-taxable-income limitation on using a post-2017 NOL in a later year, or state conformity -- that is a case to bring to a tax professional.

Is this the same as amending my 2022-2024 returns directly?

No. A separate, fully retroactive election existed under the same Rev. Proc. to amend 2022-2024 returns directly, but its election window closed July 6, 2026. This calculator only compares the two elections still available on the 2025 return -- the full-balance-in-2025 option and the split-over-2025-2026 option -- which is the live choice a small business faces right now.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the two published Rev. Proc. 2025-28 catch-up election structures to the numbers you enter. It does not verify your small-business eligibility, does not model net operating loss carryforward value, does not know your complete tax return, and is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you elect either option.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your business's small-business eligibility and your own numbers before electing either option on a filed return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also opening a savings account for a child this year? See the Trump Account calculator — a different brand-new 2025-2026 OBBBA provision, same "no signup, run the numbers yourself" shape.

Working this out by hand instead? See where a hand estimate of the 174A catch-up usually goes wrong.

Want to see the 1-year-vs-2-year math worked all the way through? See should I take the 174A catch-up in one year or two?, including why a weak 2025 can make the 1-year path waste most of the deduction into an unmodeled NOL.

Also doing R&D? The R&D tax credit calculator estimates the separate Section 41 credit and its payroll-tax offset.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Should I take the Section 174A catch-up in one year or two?

The election is a real financial tradeoff, not a formality -- and the answer depends far more on your income in each year than most summaries suggest. Three worked examples below, all pinned to this calculator's own arithmetic, on the same $200,000 remaining unamortized balance.

Worked example 1: equal rates both years -- a small edge to the 1-year path

$200,000 remaining balance, $500,000 of taxable income in both 2025 and 2026, a flat 21% rate both years, 6% annual discount rate.

Line1-year path2-year path
2025 deduction claimed$200,000$100,000
2026 deduction claimed$0$100,000
2025 cash savings$42,000.00$21,000.00
2026 cash savings$0.00$21,000.00
Nominal total$42,000.00$42,000.00
Present value at 6%/year$42,000.00$40,811.32

Same $42,000 nominal total either way -- the 1-year path only wins because that money arrives entirely in 2025 instead of split across two years. Present-value edge: $1,188.68 (2.83%) in the 1-year path's favor, from time value of money alone.

Worked example 2: a weak 2025 changes everything

Same $200,000 balance and the same 21% rate both years, but 2025 taxable income before this deduction is only $20,000 -- a near-breakeven year -- while 2026 is back to $500,000.

Line1-year path2-year path
2025 deduction claimed / usable$200,000 / $20,000$100,000 / $20,000
2025 excess (creates/increases an NOL)$180,000$80,000
2025 cash savings$4,200.00$4,200.00
2026 deduction claimed / usable$0 / $0$100,000 / $100,000
2026 cash savings$0.00$21,000.00
Nominal total$4,200.00$25,200.00
Present value at 6%/year$4,200.00$24,011.32

The 1-year path can only use $20,000 of its $200,000 deduction against 2025's thin income -- the other $180,000 does not vanish, but it becomes an NOL question this calculator does not model, instead of a cash saving today. The 2-year path wastes less into that same NOL gap in 2025 (only $80,000 excess against its smaller $100,000 claim) and puts its full second half to work against 2026's healthy income. Present-value gap: $19,811.32 -- nearly five times the 1-year path's total -- in the 2-year path's favor.

Worked example 3: an expected 2026 rate increase flips example 1

Same $200,000 balance, same $500,000 of income both years as example 1 -- but the business expects its marginal rate to rise from 21% in 2025 to 30% in 2026.

Line1-year path2-year path
Present value at 6%/year$42,000.00$49,301.89

Nothing about the income or the balance changed from example 1 -- only the expected 2026 rate did. That alone is enough to flip the present-value edge from +$1,188.68 for the 1-year path to +$7,301.89 for the 2-year path, because each dollar deducted in 2026 is now worth more per dollar than one deducted in 2025.

Run this with your own numbers

The Section 174A catch-up calculator runs this same present-value comparison on your own remaining balance, income, rates, and discount rate, and flags whenever a deduction would exceed a year's taxable income. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

If my tax rate will be the same both years, does it matter which path I pick?

A little, in the 1-year path's favor. On a $200,000 balance at a flat 21% rate both years and $500,000 of income each year, the 1-year path's $42,000 in savings arrives entirely in 2025, while the 2-year path's identical $42,000 nominal total splits $21,000/$21,000 across 2025 and 2026. Discounted at 6%/year, getting money sooner is worth about $1,188.68 more today -- a real but modest edge from time value of money alone.

What if 2025 is a weak year for my business?

This is where the two paths can diverge sharply. On the same $200,000 balance, if 2025 taxable income before this deduction is only $20,000, the 1-year path can only use $20,000 of the $200,000 deduction that year -- the remaining $180,000 does not vanish, but it creates or increases a net operating loss instead of an immediate cash saving, worth just $4,200 up front. The 2-year path claims $100,000 in 2025 (also capped at the $20,000 usable that year, so it wastes less into NOL territory on that half) and the other $100,000 in 2026 against a healthy $500,000 of income, capturing a full $21,000 there. Total nominal savings: $4,200 for the 1-year path versus $25,200 for the 2-year path -- a present-value gap of about $19,811.32 in the 2-year path's favor.

What if I expect my tax rate to go up in 2026?

An expected rate increase independently favors the 2-year path, because the half deducted in 2026 is then worth more per dollar. On the same $200,000 balance at $500,000 of income both years, moving the 2026 rate from 21% to 30% flips the present-value edge from the 1-year path (+$1,188.68) to the 2-year path (+$7,301.89) -- a rate change alone is enough to change which election is better, even though nothing about the income or the balance changed.

vs-doing-the-math-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. working out the Section 174A catch-up by hand

The 174A catch-up looks like one multiplication — a balance times a tax rate. The problem is that both the "cap it at taxable income" rule and the time-value difference between 2025 and 2026 are easy to skip when you are doing the arithmetic once, in a spreadsheet cell, rather than running both election paths side by side.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Capping the deductionMultiplies the full deduction by the tax rate, even when the deduction is bigger than that year's taxable income.Caps the usable deduction at that year's taxable income before the deduction, and flags the excess as an NOL risk rather than counting it as cash saved.
Comparing the two pathsCompares nominal dollars only, missing that a 2025 dollar is worth more than a 2026 dollar.Computes the present value of each path's combined savings at an adjustable discount rate, and states the dollar and percentage difference.
Which election this even isConfuses the 2025-return 1-year/2-year choice with the separate retroactive election to amend 2022-2024 returns, whose window closed July 6, 2026.Only models the live 2025-return choice, and says so explicitly.
Rate assumptionsAssumes the same rate in both years, even when a bracket change is expected.Takes separate 2025 and 2026 rates and income, and names when the two disagree enough to matter.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Forgetting that a deduction can only produce an immediate cash tax saving up to that year's taxable income before the deduction. A hand estimate often multiplies the whole deduction by the tax rate and calls that the saving -- but if the deduction is bigger than the year's income, the excess does not vanish or convert to cash; it can create or increase a net operating loss instead, which is a different (and generally less valuable) outcome.

What's the second most common mistake?

Comparing the two elections on nominal dollars alone. If your 2025 and 2026 rates and income are similar, the 1-year and 2-year paths can add up to about the same total tax saving on paper -- but a dollar saved in 2025 is worth more than a dollar saved in 2026, so a nominal-only comparison misses the time-value difference between the two paths.

What election-scope mistake gets made most often?

Confusing the 1-year-vs-2-year choice on the 2025 return with the separate retroactive election to amend 2022-2024 returns directly. That retroactive path existed under the same Rev. Proc. 2025-28, but its election window closed July 6, 2026. The live choice today is only between taking the remaining balance entirely in 2025 or splitting it across 2025-2026.

What rate mistake gets made most often?

Assuming the same marginal or effective rate applies in both years. A business anticipating a bracket change -- higher income, a change in entity structure, or a different mix of income -- can get a meaningfully different answer than one assuming a flat rate, and a hand estimate often skips modeling the two years separately.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, AMT, self-employment tax, or state conformity to Section 174A, which varies by state. Neither verifies your small-business eligibility (the $31 million average-gross-receipts test) or models net operating loss carryforward value. Both apply the same published Rev. Proc. 2025-28 election structures to the numbers you enter; verify against the IRS's own guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.
